tagline: Write a word in chalk and the wall obeys it, while a ten-second bell keeps changing the rules.
overview: Drowsy Orchestra is a first-person puzzle walk through a sleeping clock hall. Three big walls block the way. Beside each one lie pieces of chalk, and each piece is a word: pick it up and the word is written on the wall, and the wall starts behaving like that word. MELT makes it flow open for a while, LOW shrinks it to a step you can hop, STILL freezes the clock-faced beast that patrols the hall. Every ten seconds a bell rings and you choose one of three laws that change how everything behaves. The fewest words and the fewest lost minutes make the quietest run.
story: The clockmaker stopped time in his great hall and then vanished. You are his last apprentice, and the only thing you still know is his old trick: chalk a word on a wall and the wall remembers what the word means. At the far end of the hall waits the Stopped Clock. Between you and it stand three walls, a bell that keeps the hall awake, and the Tock, a clock-faced beast that eats a minute of your day every time it catches you.
goal: Walk through the hall to the Stopped Clock at the far end. You win when you reach it; try to do it with as few words as you can. You lose if the Tock catches you five times: the day is gone.
rules: Pick up a piece of chalk (E) to write its word on the wall in front of you; each word you write counts against you.
MELT: the wall melts and you can walk through, but it closes again after a few seconds (never on top of you).
LOW: the wall shrinks to a low step that stays; jump over it.
STILL (last room only): the Tock freezes for six seconds.

From the second room on, a bell rings every ten seconds. Choose one law: left-click for Hush (slow Tock, walls close fast), right-click for Loud (fast Tock, walls stay open longer) or Ctrl for Sleep (no Tock, but every word counts twice).

If you step into a column of the orange band while the Tock is on it, or the Tock moves onto your column and you then step out, it catches you: you lose one minute and return to the start of the room. Five lost minutes ends the run.

controls.action: pick up chalk and write its word on the wall
when the bell rings: choose the law Hush / Loud / Sleep

characters.name: The Apprentice
characters.description: You, the clockmaker's last apprentice. You carry nothing but a conductor's baton and a head full of words.

characters.name: The Tock
characters.description: A clock-faced beast on brass legs. It paces along the orange band one step at a time and eats a minute of your day if it catches you.

characters.name: MELT chalk
characters.description: Orange chalk on a slate plinth. Writing MELT makes a wall flow away for a few seconds.

characters.name: STILL chalk
characters.description: Blue chalk found in the last room. Writing STILL stops the Tock in its tracks for six seconds.

characters.name: The Bell
characters.description: A brass bell hanging in the hall. It rings every ten seconds and forces you to pick a new law.

characters.name: The Walls
characters.description: Three heavy purple walls with a word floating above each. They do whatever the word says.

tips: Wait for the Tock to pass your column, then cross the orange band right behind it.
LOW is cheap and permanent; MELT is free to walk through but runs out.
Sleep makes the Tock harmless but doubles every word, so pick it before you cross, not before you write.

why_made: The card wanted me to write a word on a wall and have the wall obey, with a bell forcing a new choice every ten seconds. I kept the writing as the whole game, but made it physical: each word is a piece of chalk you pick up, so the verb is just walking up and pressing E. I turned the three laws into a quick click choice with the bell, because a menu would have stopped the action. I dropped the open-ended 'any word you like' because the engine cannot read typed text, so I gave you three words that really do different things, and I made the beast a patrolling clock so the danger is visible. The scoring is the card's own idea: fewest words wins.
